questions.topic: Bird notes high, bear notes low
questions.prompt: Your teacher plays a sound that is high like a little bird. Where on the piano would you find bird notes like that?
choices: the keys at the far right end of the keyboard
the keys at the far left end of the keyboard
the white keys in the very middle only
any key that you press extra hard
questions.answer: the keys at the far right end of the keyboard
questions.rationale: Bird notes are high sounds, and the high sounds come from the far right end of the keyboard.

questions.topic: Sit at the middle of the keys
questions.prompt: When you sit down to play the piano, where should your body be?
choices: in the middle of the keyboard, so both ends are easy to reach
at the far left end, right next to the low keys
at the far right end, right next to the high keys
as far back from the keyboard as your arms can reach
questions.answer: in the middle of the keyboard, so both ends are easy to reach
questions.rationale: A pianist sits in the middle of the keys so the whole keyboard is within easy reach.

questions.prompt: When you get your hand ready to play, what shape should your fingers be in?
choices: stretched out flat and stiff
squeezed tightly into a fist
rounded, as if holding a bubble that must not pop
spread apart in a straight line
questions.answer: rounded, as if holding a bubble that must not pop
questions.rationale: Bubble hands keep the fingers gently rounded, the way they would curl around a bubble.

questions.topic: Play the finger I call out
questions.prompt: In your lesson the teacher calls out, "Play with finger 4." Which finger do you play with?
choices: your pointing finger
your tallest middle finger
your smallest pinky finger
your ring finger
questions.answer: your ring finger
questions.rationale: With the thumb counted as finger 1, finger 4 is the ring finger.

questions.prompt: You play three black keys in a row, starting near the left side of the keyboard and moving toward the right. How does your music change?
choices: it goes up, note by note
it goes down, note by note
it stays on one repeated note
it gets quieter each time
questions.answer: it goes up, note by note
questions.rationale: Moving to the right on the keyboard makes the notes higher, so the music goes up.

questions.topic: Hammers hit strings inside the piano
questions.prompt: When you press a piano key, what makes the sound inside the piano?
choices: the key rubs against the wooden case and squeaks
a small hammer inside swings up and strikes a string
air is blown through a pipe behind the key
two keys press against each other and click
questions.answer: a small hammer inside swings up and strikes a string
questions.rationale: Pressing a key swings a felt-covered hammer against a string, and the vibrating string makes the sound.

questions.topic: Hot Cross Buns on three black keys
questions.prompt: At your living-room concert you play the first line of Hot Cross Buns on black keys: you start on the highest key of a group of three and step to the middle one, then the lowest one. Which keys did you use, and did the music go up or down?
choices: the group of two black keys, and the music went up
the group of three black keys, and the music went up
the group of three black keys, and the music went down
the group of two black keys, and the music went down
questions.answer: the group of three black keys, and the music went down
questions.rationale: Hot Cross Buns lives on the group of three black keys, and stepping from the top key to the middle to the bottom makes the music go down.

questions.prompt: In your lesson you make one sound by holding a key down for a long time, and another sound by touching a key for only a moment. What do musicians call the difference between those two sounds?
choices: high and low
loud and soft
long and short
fast and slow
questions.answer: long and short
questions.rationale: How long a sound lasts is its length, so the two sounds were long and short.

questions.prompt: The letter names used in music go A, B, C, D, E, F, G and then start over. If you climb up the piano naming white keys and you have just said "G", which letter do you say next?
choices: A
H
F
C
questions.answer: A
questions.rationale: The musical alphabet stops at G and wraps around, so the letter after G is A.

questions.topic: finding C from the black-key groups
questions.prompt: Every C on the piano sits in the same spot in the pattern of black keys. What should you look for right next to a key to know it is a C?
choices: a group of three black keys, just to its right
a group of two black keys, just to its right
a group of two black keys, just to its left
one black key standing alone, just to its right
questions.answer: a group of two black keys, just to its right
questions.rationale: Every white key sitting immediately to the left of a pair of two black keys is a C.

questions.prompt: A whole note holds for four beats and a half note holds for two beats. How many half notes fill the same amount of time as one whole note?
choices: one half note
two half notes
three half notes
four half notes
questions.answer: two half notes
questions.rationale: Two half notes of two beats each add up to the whole note's four beats.

questions.topic: sharps raise a note to the next key up
questions.prompt: Your music shows a C with a sharp sign in front of it. Where on the piano do you find C sharp?
choices: the white key D, the next letter up from C
the next white C higher up the keyboard
the black key just down and to the left of the white key C
the black key just up and to the right of the white key C
questions.answer: the black key just up and to the right of the white key C
questions.rationale: A sharp raises a note to the very next key up, which from the white key C is the black key to its right.

questions.prompt: You press a key, hold the damper pedal down, and then lift your finger off while the pedal stays down. What happens to the sound?
choices: It keeps ringing until you lift your foot off the pedal.
It stops the moment your finger leaves the key, just like playing without the pedal.
It changes to a much softer ringing until your finger comes back down.
It goes silent and only rings again once you press the pedal a second time.
questions.answer: It keeps ringing until you lift your foot off the pedal.
questions.rationale: The damper pedal holds the dampers off the strings, so the note keeps ringing until you release the pedal.

questions.prompt: You count “1 2 3 4” for a 4/4 measure and play the right‑hand C five‑finger pattern (C‑D‑E‑F‑G) using quarter notes on beats 1 and 2, then a half note that covers beats 3‑4. Which finger plays the half note?
choices: Finger 1 (C) plays the half note.
Finger 3 (E) plays the half note.
Finger 4 (F) plays the half note.
Finger 5 (G) plays the half note.
questions.answer: Finger 3 (E) plays the half note.
questions.rationale: Quarter notes on beats 1 and 2 use fingers 1 (C) and 2 (D). The half note begins on beat 3, which corresponds to the third note of the pattern, E, played with finger 3.

questions.topic: Three Guide Notes: Bass F, Middle C, Treble G
questions.prompt: The three guide notes you learn first are Bass F, Middle C and Treble G. When Middle C is written for the right hand, where does it sit?
choices: on the bottom line of the treble staff
in the space just under the treble staff
on its own short line drawn just below the treble staff
on the top line of the bass staff
questions.answer: on its own short line drawn just below the treble staff
questions.rationale: Middle C for the right hand sits on its own small extra line just below the treble staff, which is what makes it a guide note.

questions.prompt: Your new piece is marked "legato" at the top. How should the notes sound under your fingers?
choices: short and detached, with a tiny silence between each note
smooth and connected, with no silence between notes
very loud, with a strong attack on every note
very slow, with a breath after every two notes
questions.answer: smooth and connected, with no silence between notes
questions.rationale: Legato means playing smoothly so each note connects to the next with no gap of silence between them.

questions.topic: Identifying stepwise motion on the staff
questions.prompt: On the treble staff a note appears on the second line (G). The very next note is written in the space directly above that line. What interval does this represent?
choices: The melody moves up by a step.
The melody moves up by a skip.
The melody repeats the same pitch.
The melody leaps up an octave.
questions.answer: The melody moves up by a step.
questions.rationale: A line‑to‑adjacent‑space move is a diatonic step. A skip would be line‑to‑line or space‑to‑space, a repeat stays on the same line/space, and an octave leap spans seven steps.

questions.prompt: In a piece in three time, a bar begins with two quarter notes on beats one and two, and a quarter rest sits on beat three. What do you do during beat three?
choices: you stop counting and wait for the next bar line
you play beat three as a very soft note
you jump straight to the first note of the next bar
you keep counting silently and play nothing
questions.answer: you keep counting silently and play nothing
questions.rationale: A rest is a counted silence: the pulse keeps going with your counting, but no key is played.

questions.topic: Sharps, Flats and Naturals Last the Whole Bar
questions.prompt: In one bar you see a flat sign in front of the very first B. Two more B notes follow later in that same bar with no signs in front of them. How do you play those two later B notes?
choices: both as B natural, since they have no flat sign of their own
both as B flat, since the flat lasts to the end of the bar
the first as B flat and the second as B natural
the first as B natural and the second as B flat
questions.answer: both as B flat, since the flat lasts to the end of the bar
questions.rationale: An accidental such as a flat stays in force for every note of the same name until the end of the bar, so both later B notes are played as B flat.

questions.prompt: When playing the D major pentascale (D‑E‑F♯‑G‑A) with the right hand in the standard fingering, which finger plays the note G?
choices: Finger 2 plays G.
Finger 3 plays G.
Finger 5 plays G.
Finger 4 plays G.
questions.answer: Finger 4 plays G.
questions.rationale: The standard right‑hand fingering for the D major pentascale assigns fingers 1‑5 to D‑E‑F♯‑G‑A respectively; therefore G is played with finger 4.

questions.topic: C Major Scale One Octave With Thumb Under
questions.prompt: You play the C major scale one octave upward with your right hand, starting with your thumb on Middle C and using the standard fingering. After finger 3 plays E, what happens next?
choices: the second finger crosses over the hand to play F
the hand jumps so that the thumb lands on F
the thumb passes under the hand to play F
the fourth finger reaches across to play F
questions.answer: the thumb passes under the hand to play F
questions.rationale: In the standard right-hand C major scale, the thumb passes under the hand after finger 3 plays E so it can reach F and continue smoothly up the octave.

questions.prompt: In 4/4 time, two beamed eighth notes appear together. How many beats do those two eighth notes together occupy?
choices: Half a beat
One beat
Two beats
A quarter beat
questions.answer: One beat
questions.rationale: Two eighth notes equal one quarter note, which receives one beat in 4/4 time.

questions.prompt: When the right hand moves from finger 3 to finger 1 while playing a scale, the thumb passes under the hand. What is the purpose of this motion?
choices: To create a staccato articulation
To increase the dynamic level
To avoid using finger 4
To reach the next note smoothly
questions.answer: To reach the next note smoothly
questions.rationale: The thumb‑under motion allows a seamless connection to the next higher note without interrupting the line.

questions.prompt: A major scale is built from a specific pattern of whole steps (tones) and half steps (semitones). Starting on the tonic, what is that pattern?
choices: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
Whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole
Half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole
Whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half
questions.answer: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
questions.rationale: The major scale follows the interval sequence W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑H from the tonic.

questions.prompt: One ledger line placed above the treble staff corresponds to which pitch?
choices: G5
C6
A5
E5
questions.answer: A5
questions.rationale: The top line of the treble staff is F5; the space above is G5, and the first ledger line above that is A5.

questions.prompt: Which major key signature contains exactly one sharp?
choices: D major
F major
G major
C major
questions.answer: G major
questions.rationale: G major has a single sharp (F♯) in its key signature.

questions.prompt: A tie connects two notes of the same pitch across a bar line. What is the resulting effect on the sound?
choices: The notes are played separately with a slight break
The notes are played as a single sustained note
The notes become staccato
The pitch changes by a semitone
questions.answer: The notes are played as a single sustained note
questions.rationale: A tie adds the durations of the tied notes, producing one continuous tone.

questions.prompt: In D natural minor, what is the interval between the tonic (D) and the sixth scale degree?
choices: Perfect fifth
Major sixth
Minor seventh
Minor sixth
questions.answer: Minor sixth
questions.rationale: The sixth degree of D natural minor is B♭, which forms a minor sixth above the tonic D.

questions.prompt: In the standard fingering for the G major scale played two octaves ascending with the right hand, which finger plays the first note of the second octave?
choices: index finger (2)
thumb (1)
middle finger (3)
ring finger (4)
questions.answer: thumb (1)
questions.rationale: The two‑octave G major scale restarts the fingering pattern at the beginning of the second octave, so the thumb plays the first note again.

questions.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fit into the duration of a single quarter note?
choices: two
three
four
five
questions.answer: four
questions.rationale: A quarter note equals two eighth notes, and each eighth note contains two sixteenth notes, giving four sixteenth notes per quarter note.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended alignment of the hand, wrist, and forearm when playing at the keyboard?
choices: they should form a straight line
the wrist should be noticeably higher than the forearm
the forearm should be noticeably higher than the wrist
they should form a gentle upward curve
questions.answer: they should form a straight line
questions.rationale: A straight line from hand through wrist to forearm promotes efficient motion and reduces tension.

questions.prompt: A note written on the second ledger line above the treble staff corresponds to which pitch?
choices: A5
B5
C6
D6
questions.answer: C6
questions.rationale: The first ledger line above the treble staff is A5; the second ledger line is the next space up, C6.

questions.prompt: In the I‑V‑vi‑IV progression in G major, what is the vi chord?
choices: A minor
B minor
C♯ minor
E minor
questions.answer: E minor
questions.rationale: The vi chord is built on the sixth scale degree; in G major the sixth degree is E, giving an E minor triad.

questions.prompt: An Alberti bass pattern in C major typically outlines the chord tones in which order?
choices: root, third, fifth, third
root, fifth, third, fifth
third, root, fifth, root
fifth, root, third, root
questions.answer: root, fifth, third, fifth
questions.rationale: The classic Alberti bass alternates low–high–middle–high, i.e., root, fifth, third, fifth.

questions.topic: Comprehensive practice routine covering all Elementary 2 skills
questions.prompt: Which weekly routine demonstrates mastery of every Elementary 2 skill: two‑octave G major scale hands together, sixteenth‑note groupings, two‑ledger‑line sight‑reading, I‑V‑vi‑IV loops in C G F, Alberti bass drills, and legato pedal changes?
choices: A routine that adds chord loops and pedal work but omits ledger‑line reading.
A routine that includes scales, sixteenth drills, ledger reading, chord loops in three keys, Alberti bass, and pedal work.
A routine that focuses only on scales and arpeggios without chords or pedal.
A routine that skips pedal work and Alberti bass while keeping other items.
questions.answer: A routine that includes scales, sixteenth drills, ledger reading, chord loops in three keys, Alberti bass, and pedal work.
questions.rationale: Only the second description contains every listed element; the others each miss at least one required component.

questions.prompt: How many flats does the key signature of B-flat major have, and which are they?
choices: Two: B-flat and E-flat
Two: B-flat and A-flat
Three: B-flat, E-flat and A-flat
One: B-flat
questions.answer: Two: B-flat and E-flat
questions.rationale: B-flat major has two flats, B-flat and E-flat (flats are added in the order B, E, A, D...); three flats is E-flat major.

questions.topic: First structural label when mapping a long piece
questions.prompt: When you begin to map a lengthy composition, what is the highest‑level division you label first?
choices: Phrases
Movements
Sections
Measures
questions.answer: Sections
questions.rationale: Mapping starts with large formal sections (e.g., exposition, development). Phrases and measures are lower‑level, and movements apply only to multi‑movement works.

questions.topic: Build the melodic minor up and down
questions.prompt: In the melodic minor scale, the sixth and seventh degrees are raised on the way up and lowered on the way down. Which pattern of whole and half steps represents the ascending form?
choices: W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑W‑H
W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑H
W‑W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑H
W‑W‑W‑W‑H‑W‑H
questions.answer: W‑W‑H‑W‑W‑W‑H
questions.rationale: The ascending melodic minor follows whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half steps.

questions.topic: Key signatures up to four sharps and flats
questions.prompt: A key signature with four flats corresponds to which major key?
choices: A‑flat major
E‑flat major
B‑flat major
F major
questions.answer: A‑flat major
questions.rationale: Four flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭) define the key of A‑flat major.

questions.topic: Identifying key from accidentals without a key signature
questions.prompt: A melody written without a key signature contains the notes F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯ and no flats. Which major key does this imply?
choices: E major
A major
D major
G major
questions.answer: E major
questions.rationale: Four sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯) define the key of E major. A major has three, D major two, G major one.

questions.topic: Double Sharps and Double Flats on the Keys
questions.prompt: In a passage written in the key of B major, a double sharp appears before the note A. Which pitch is actually sounded?
choices: A♯
B
B♯
C
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: A double sharp raises a note by two semitones; A → A♯ → B natural.

questions.topic: Transpose a melody, sus4 chords, and ornament signs
questions.prompt: To transpose a melody from G major to E‑flat major, add a suspended fourth chord on the subdominant, and apply a mordent on the tonic note, which set of skills from this grade must be combined?
choices: Scale transposition, triad inversion, and grace‑note execution
Key‑signature identification, chord‑colour recognition, and ornament interpretation
Interval calculation, lead‑sheet reading, and tempo‑modifier application
Rhythm dictation, contrary‑motion scaling, and dynamic shaping
questions.answer: Key‑signature identification, chord‑colour recognition, and ornament interpretation
questions.rationale: Transposing requires knowing key signatures, adding a sus4 needs chord‑colour knowledge, and a mordent demands ornament interpretation.

questions.topic: Where Finger Four Falls: Scale Fingering Rules
questions.prompt: In the standard right‑hand fingering for any major scale, which scale degree is always played by finger 4?
choices: 2nd
4th
6th
7th
questions.answer: 7th
questions.rationale: The fingering rule taught in this grade states that finger 4 consistently plays the leading‑tone (7th degree) in major scales.

questions.topic: Key signatures up to five sharps
questions.prompt: Which major key signature contains exactly five sharps?
choices: F♯ major
B major
C♯ major
G major
questions.answer: B major
questions.rationale: The key of B major has five sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯).

questions.topic: Pedal changes guided by bass harmony
questions.prompt: When the bass line in a piece moves from a tonic chord to a dominant seventh chord, what is the most appropriate pedal action?
choices: Lift the pedal completely and re‑depress on the new harmony
Keep the pedal down throughout the change
Change the pedal only on the downbeat of the new measure
Use the una corda pedal instead of the sustain pedal
questions.answer: Lift the pedal completely and re‑depress on the new harmony
questions.rationale: A harmony change from tonic to dominant seventh requires a clean pedal change to avoid blurring the new chord.

questions.topic: Counting through rests in compound meter
questions.prompt: A measure in 6/8 contains a dotted quarter note followed by an eighth rest and then three eighth notes. How many beats does the dotted quarter note occupy?
choices: One beat
Two beats
Three beats
Half a beat
questions.answer: One beat
questions.rationale: In 6/8 the beat unit is a dotted quarter note, which equals three eighth‑note pulses, i.e., one beat.

questions.topic: Technical name of the fourth scale degree
questions.prompt: In a major scale, what is the technical name for the fourth scale degree?
choices: The fourth degree is called the dominant.
The fourth degree is called the mediant.
The fourth degree is called the supertonic.
The fourth degree is called the subdominant.
questions.answer: The fourth degree is called the subdominant.
questions.rationale: Scale‑degree names: 1 tonic, 2 supertonic, 3 mediant, 4 subdominant, 5 dominant. The distractors are the names of other degrees.

questions.prompt: In the harmonic minor version of F♯ minor, what is the pitch of the raised seventh degree?
choices: E
E♯
F
F♯
questions.answer: E♯
questions.rationale: The natural minor seventh is E; raising it a semitone gives E♯ (enharmonic to F natural but spelled E♯).

questions.topic: Integrated performance practice: cadential progression, Alberti bass, simile sig
questions.prompt: A short excerpt in 6/8 time begins with an anacrusis of a single eighth note, then presents a I‑IV‑V⁶⁴‑⁵³‑I cadential progression in E‑flat major, followed by a brief Alberti bass in the left hand that uses forearm rotation, and ends with a simile sign indicating the previous articulation continues. Which of the following describes the correct performance practice for this excerpt?
choices: Play the anacrusis on the upbeat, execute the cadential chords with a slight ritardando, use forearm rotation for the Alberti bass, and maintain the articulation through the simile sign.
Play the anacrusis on the downbeat, execute the cadential chords strictly in tempo, use finger‑only Alberti bass, and change articulation at the simile sign.
Play the anacrusis on the upbeat, execute the cadential chords with a sudden forte, use wrist rotation for the Alberti bass, and ignore the simile sign.
Play the anacrusis on the downbeat, execute the cadential chords with a slight accelerando, use forearm rotation for the Alberti bass, and maintain the articulation through the simile sign.
questions.answer: Play the anacrusis on the upbeat, execute the cadential chords with a slight ritardando, use forearm rotation for the Alberti bass, and maintain the articulation through the simile sign.
questions.rationale: The anacrusis falls on the upbeat, the cadential progression traditionally relaxes slightly, forearm rotation is the prescribed technique for Alberti bass at this level, and a simile sign means the preceding articulation continues.

questions.topic: Circle of fifths and key signatures
questions.prompt: When moving clockwise around the circle of fifths, each step adds which accidental to the key signature?
choices: One flat is added
One sharp is added
Two sharps are added
Two flats are added
questions.answer: One sharp is added
questions.rationale: Each clockwise step on the circle of fifths raises the key by a perfect fifth, which adds a single sharp to the signature.

questions.prompt: In 5/8 time, how many eighth‑note beats are contained in each measure?
choices: Four
Six
Seven
Five
questions.answer: Five
questions.rationale: The top number of a time signature indicates the number of beats per measure; 5/8 therefore has five eighth‑note beats.

questions.topic: Baroque trills starting from the upper note
questions.prompt: A Baroque trill written on the note D (just above middle C) begins on which pitch?
choices: E
D
C
F
questions.answer: E
questions.rationale: Baroque performance practice starts a trill on the upper auxiliary note, so a trill on D begins on E.

questions.prompt: Which fingering pattern is commonly recommended for a trill between G and A using fingers 4 and 5 in the right hand?
questions.rationale: Upper‑intermediate pedagogy assigns the 4‑5 pair for trills a whole step apart when the hand is positioned for speed and evenness.

questions.prompt: In a dominant seventh arpeggio built on G, which four notes are played in root position?
choices: G‑B‑D‑F
G‑B‑D‑E
G‑A‑C‑E
G‑B‑C‑F
questions.answer: G‑B‑D‑F
questions.rationale: A dominant seventh chord consists of root, major third, perfect fifth, and minor seventh; on G these are G, B, D, and F.

questions.topic: Common tone between I and IV
questions.prompt: When voice‑leading a I‑IV‑V‑I progression in C major while retaining common tones, which single note is common to both the I and IV chords?
choices: C
E
G
A
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: The I chord (C‑E‑G) and the IV chord (F‑A‑C) share only the note C.

questions.prompt: A pianist who has completed every Upper Intermediate unit will be able to do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Play all twelve major scales around the circle of fifths from memory
Execute Baroque trills beginning on the upper auxiliary note using fingers 4‑5
Perform a steady two‑against‑three cross‑rhythm at performance tempo
Improvise a jazz solo employing altered dominant chords
questions.answer: Improvise a jazz solo employing altered dominant chords
questions.rationale: The Upper Intermediate curriculum covers scales, Baroque trills, and two‑against‑three polyrhythms, but jazz improvisation with altered dominants is introduced only at later advanced levels.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended forearm position relative to the keyboard when the bench height is set correctly for a four‑octave reach?
choices: Forearms slope downward so wrists sit below the keys.
Forearms are angled upward so elbows are well below the keys.
Forearms are parallel to the floor with elbows slightly above the keys.
Forearms are vertical with wrists level with the keys.
questions.answer: Forearms are parallel to the floor with elbows slightly above the keys.
questions.rationale: Standard piano ergonomics call for the forearms to be horizontal (parallel to the floor) and the elbows a little higher than the keyboard, allowing relaxed shoulders and level wrists.

questions.prompt: In the standard right‑hand fingering for a four‑octave D‑major scale played hands together, which finger plays the first D of each octave?
choices: Finger 2 (index)
Finger 3 (middle)
Finger 1 (thumb)
Finger 4 (ring)
questions.answer: Finger 1 (thumb)
questions.rationale: The right‑hand D‑major scale begins each octave with the thumb (finger 1); the pattern 1‑2‑3‑1‑2‑3‑4 repeats every octave, so the first note of every octave is always played by the thumb.

questions.prompt: A contrary-motion scale starts with both thumbs on the same middle C. How do the hands move from there?
choices: The hands go up together, keeping an octave apart
The right hand goes down while the left hand stays where it is
The hands go down together, keeping a third apart
The right hand goes up while the left hand goes down, mirroring each other
questions.answer: The right hand goes up while the left hand goes down, mirroring each other
questions.rationale: In contrary motion the hands move in opposite directions from the shared starting note, so the fingering mirrors (thumb with thumb); in similar motion both hands move the same way.

questions.topic: Bach Sinfonia in C Minor BWV 788: opening entries
questions.prompt: In the opening of Bach’s Sinfonia in C minor (BWV 788), the subject first appears in which voice?
choices: The subject first appears in the bass (lowest voice).
The subject first appears in the tenor (lower middle voice).
The subject first appears in the soprano (upper voice).
The subject first appears in the alto (middle voice).
questions.answer: The subject first appears in the soprano (upper voice).
questions.rationale: The sinfonia’s subject enters in the top voice before being imitated in lower voices.

questions.topic: Dominant sevenths in every inversion with their figures
questions.prompt: A dominant seventh chord in second inversion (V⁴₃) has which chord tone in the bass?
choices: The root of the chord is placed in the bass.
The fifth of the chord is placed in the bass.
The third of the chord is placed in the bass.
The seventh of the chord is placed in the bass.
questions.answer: The fifth of the chord is placed in the bass.
questions.rationale: Second inversion of a seventh chord puts the fifth in the bass, shown by the 4‑3 figuring.

questions.topic: Dominant seventh second inversion figured bass
questions.prompt: When realizing a dominant seventh chord in second inversion (V⁴₃) in four‑part writing, which figured‑bass symbol appears above the bass note?
questions.rationale: A dominant seventh in second inversion has the third of the chord in the bass; the intervals above the bass are a fourth and a third, giving the figured‑bass symbol 4/3.

questions.topic: Complete performance preparation including stage dress, bench adjustment, and pe
questions.prompt: Which of the following sequences best reflects the final week of preparation for a full recital program at the Early Advanced level?
choices: Polish each piece, rehearse transitions, simulate concert conditions, adjust bench and attire, perform for a small audience.
Memorize all repertoire, record each piece, analyze recordings, rest the day before, skip warm‑up on concert day.
Focus only on the most difficult passage, practice it repeatedly, ignore easier sections, wear new shoes, arrive late.
Run through the program once, change bench height each piece, improvise cadenzas, skip bow practice, eat a heavy meal before playing.
questions.answer: Polish each piece, rehearse transitions, simulate concert conditions, adjust bench and attire, perform for a small audience.
questions.rationale: A balanced final‑week plan integrates polishing, run‑throughs, simulated performance, physical setup, and a low‑stakes audience test.

questions.prompt: In a rounded binary movement, the first reprise typically ends with a cadence in the dominant key. What is the conventional name for this cadence?
choices: Perfect authentic cadence in the dominant
Half cadence in the tonic
Deceptive cadence to the submediant
Plagal cadence in the relative minor
questions.answer: Perfect authentic cadence in the dominant
questions.rationale: Tests knowledge of binary-form cadential practice (U1). The correct option matches the standard term; distractors are other cadence types a student might confuse.

questions.prompt: When a secondary dominant (V⁷/IV) resolves, which chord does it most commonly move to in a major key?
choices: The subdominant (IV)
The mediant (iii)
The supertonic (ii)
The dominant (V)
questions.answer: The subdominant (IV)
questions.rationale: A secondary dominant of IV (V⁷/IV) functions as the dominant of the subdominant and resolves to IV.

questions.prompt: In the development of Beethoven's Sonata Op. 10 No. 1, the composer frequently uses a descending‑fifths sequence. Which harmonic pattern characterizes this sequence?
choices: Root motion down a perfect fifth, each chord a 5‑6 over the bass
Root motion up a perfect fourth, each chord a 6‑5 over the bass
Root motion down a minor third, alternating major and minor triads
Root motion up a major second, each chord a 7‑6 suspension
questions.answer: Root motion down a perfect fifth, each chord a 5‑6 over the bass
questions.rationale: A descending‑fifths (5‑6) sequence moves the bass down a fifth while the upper voice forms a 5‑6 interval over each new bass note.

questions.prompt: Which ornament, described in Couperin's L'Art de Toucher, is executed as a rapid alternation between the main note and the upper neighbor, beginning on the upper neighbor?
choices: A trill starting on the upper auxiliary
A lower mordent beginning on the main note
An inverted mordent starting on the lower auxiliary
A turn beginning on the main note
questions.answer: A trill starting on the upper auxiliary
questions.rationale: Couperin defines the trill (trille) as beginning on the note above the principal tone.

questions.prompt: When harmonizing a melody with secondary dominants at the Advanced level, the voice‑leading rule for a V⁷/vi resolving to vi requires which interval between the seventh of the secondary dominant and the third of the target chord?
choices: A descending minor second
An ascending major second
A descending major third
An ascending perfect fourth
questions.answer: A descending minor second
questions.rationale: The seventh of V⁷/vi (the leading tone of vi) resolves down a semitone to the third of vi.

questions.prompt: In C major, the chord spelled D‑F♯‑A‑C functions as which secondary dominant?
choices: V⁷/V
V⁷/IV
V⁷/vi
V⁷/ii
questions.answer: V⁷/V
questions.rationale: D⁷ is the dominant seventh of G (the dominant of C), so it is the secondary dominant V⁷/V.

questions.topic: Bach French Suite No. 5: dance-movement form
questions.prompt: In Bach's French Suite No. 5 in G major (BWV 816), what form do the dance movements such as the Allemande, Courante and Gigue share?
choices: Binary form: two repeated halves, the first moving to the dominant
Sonata form: exposition, development and recapitulation of two themes
Rondo form: a recurring refrain alternating with contrasting episodes
Theme and variations: one melody varied in each section
questions.answer: Binary form: two repeated halves, the first moving to the dominant
questions.rationale: Baroque suite dances are in binary form; in a major-key dance the first half modulates to the dominant (D major) and the second half returns to G.

questions.prompt: In a three‑voice fugue, the subject enters first in the alto, then the soprano answers a perfect fifth higher, and the bass enters with a tonal answer a fourth lower. Which term describes the soprano’s answer?
choices: Real answer
Tonal answer
Inverted answer
Stretto answer
questions.answer: Real answer
questions.rationale: A perfect‑fifth transposition preserving all intervals is a real answer, unlike a tonal answer which adjusts intervals.

questions.prompt: When practicing a chromatic scale in octaves with the right hand, the thumb and fifth finger must maintain a consistent interval while the inner fingers negotiate semitone shifts. What is the primary technical goal of this exercise?
choices: Develop even tone across the octave span
Increase wrist flexibility for wide leaps
Strengthen the fourth finger for rapid passages
Train the hand to shift position every two notes
questions.answer: Develop even tone across the octave span
questions.rationale: The octave‑chromatic exercise is designed to cultivate uniform sound and control across the full octave distance.

questions.prompt: A composer writes an augmented sixth chord resolving outward to the dominant in C minor. The chord contains the notes Ab, C, Eb, and F#. Which augmented sixth type is this?
choices: Italian sixth
French sixth
German sixth
Swiss sixth
questions.answer: German sixth
questions.rationale: The German sixth includes a perfect fifth (Eb) above the bass together with the augmented sixth (F#) and major third (C).

questions.prompt: The opening Grave of Beethoven’s Sonata Op. 13 begins with a C‑minor chord followed by a diminished seventh chord built on the leading tone. Which chord functions as the diminished seventh in this passage?
choices: B‑diminished seventh (B‑D‑F‑Ab)
G‑sharp diminished seventh (G#‑B‑D‑F)
D‑diminished seventh (D‑F‑Ab‑Cb)
E‑diminished seventh (E‑G‑Bb‑Db)
questions.answer: B‑diminished seventh (B‑D‑F‑Ab)
questions.rationale: In C minor the leading tone is B, so the diminished seventh built on B appears after the opening C‑minor chord.

questions.prompt: In a passage marked 4‑against‑5, the right hand plays five evenly spaced notes while the left hand plays four in the same duration. If the left hand plays quarter notes, what note value does each right‑hand note receive?
choices: Sixteenth note
Eighth‑note quintuplet
Quarter‑note quintuplet
Dotted eighth note
questions.answer: Quarter‑note quintuplet
questions.rationale: Five notes in the time of four quarter notes are notated as a quintuplet of quarter‑note value.

questions.prompt: In the key of C minor, an Italian augmented sixth chord resolving to the dominant (G) contains which set of pitches?
choices: A♭‑C‑E♭
A♭‑C‑F
A♭‑C‑F♯
A♭‑C‑E
questions.answer: A♭‑C‑F♯
questions.rationale: The Italian sixth in C minor is built on ♭VI (A♭) with a major third (C) and an augmented sixth (F♯) that resolves outward to the dominant G.

questions.prompt: A pianist preparing a full performance of Beethoven’s Pathétique Sonata must coordinate three large‑scale demands: (1) maintain consistent voicing across the Grave, Allegro, and Rondo; (2) execute the extended coda’s rapid octave passages without tension; (3) shape the Adagio cantabile’s melodic line while balancing the accompaniment. Which single practice strategy most directly addresses all three demands simultaneously?
choices: Slow, hands‑separate repetition of each movement
Full‑tempo run‑throughs with a metronome
Segmented mental rehearsal combined with targeted physical mapping of arm weight
Isolated technical drills for octaves, trills, and legato separately
questions.answer: Segmented mental rehearsal combined with targeted physical mapping of arm weight
questions.rationale: Integrated mental rehearsal with purposeful arm‑weight mapping unifies voicing, tension‑free octaves, and melodic shaping across the entire sonata.

questions.prompt: According to Duke and colleagues, what distinguishes effective practice from mere repetition?
choices: Practising a passage repeatedly until it feels comfortable.
Setting a specific goal, obtaining immediate feedback, and correcting errors.
Completing a fixed number of practice hours each day.
Playing the entire piece at performance tempo from the first session.
questions.answer: Setting a specific goal, obtaining immediate feedback, and correcting errors.
questions.rationale: Duke et al. define effective practice as goal‑directed, feedback‑rich, and error‑correcting rather than simple repetition.

questions.topic: Bach Prelude in D major BWV 850 without pedal (U1)
questions.prompt: When performing the Prelude in D major BWV 850 without pedal, which articulation principle guides the treatment of the successive sixteenth‑note figures?
choices: Each figure is detached with a slight lift between groups.
The figures are played legato, relying on finger overlap for continuity.
All sixteenth notes are rendered staccato to clarify the harmonic rhythm.
The performer alternates between legato and staccato every two measures.
questions.answer: The figures are played legato, relying on finger overlap for continuity.
questions.rationale: Bach’s keyboard style demands a singing line; without pedal the performer must use finger legato to connect the rapid figures.

questions.topic: Baroque ornament tables from Bach and Couperin (U2)
questions.prompt: In Couperin’s ornament table, the symbol ‘tr’ with a small slash indicates which execution?
choices: A mordent beginning on the principal note and moving to the lower neighbor.
An inverted mordent beginning on the lower auxiliary.
A rapid alternation starting on the upper auxiliary note.
A trill beginning on the principal note with a termination.
questions.answer: A rapid alternation starting on the upper auxiliary note.
questions.rationale: Couperin’s ‘tr/’ sign denotes a trill that begins on the upper neighbor, a standard French‑style trill.

questions.topic: Mozart K.332 exposition second theme key
questions.prompt: In the exposition of Mozart's Sonata in F major, K. 332, the second theme appears in which key?
choices: F major
B♭ major
C major
D minor
questions.answer: C major
questions.rationale: The exposition of a Classical sonata in a major key typically presents the second theme in the dominant; for F major the dominant is C major.

questions.topic: Partial pedalling and historical pedal marks (U7)
questions.prompt: In Schumann’s ‘Fantasiestücke’ Op. 12, a half‑pedal marking (½ Ped.) over a chord indicates which pedalling technique?
choices: Depress the sustain pedal fully, then release halfway before the next harmony.
Apply the sustain pedal only enough to blend the harmony without blurring the melody.
Engage the una corda pedal simultaneously with the sustain pedal.
Use the sostenuto pedal to hold the bass while the upper voices change.
questions.answer: Apply the sustain pedal only enough to blend the harmony without blurring the melody.
questions.rationale: A half‑pedal directs the pianist to use a shallow sustain, preserving clarity while adding warmth.

questions.topic: Chromatic chords mixed drill in random keys (U9)
questions.prompt: During a mixed‑key chromatic chord drill, a German augmented sixth chord resolves to the dominant in the key of E minor. Which chord tones constitute that German sixth?
choices: C‑E‑G‑B♭
C‑E‑G♯‑B♭
C‑E‑G‑A♯
C‑E‑G♯‑A♯
questions.answer: C‑E‑G‑A♯
questions.rationale: In E minor the German sixth is built on ♭VI (C) with an augmented sixth (A♯) above the bass, plus the major third (E) and perfect fifth (G).

questions.topic: Integration of Diploma repertoire and pedagogy (U10‑U11)
questions.prompt: A Diploma‑level pianist preparing a recital that includes Chopin’s Black‑Key Etude Op. 10 No. 5, the Mazurka Op. 17 No. 4, and the Waltz Op. 42 must demonstrate mastery of which combined skill set?
choices: Clean black‑key glissandi, Polish rubato varieties, and seamless voice‑leading in rootless voicings.
Fast octave passages, Baroque ornament realization, and accurate figured‑bass realisation.
Historical pedal markings, double‑minor‑third chromatic scales, and beginner‑lesson planning.
Four‑octave scale fluency, sonata‑form analysis, and jazz chord‑colour identification.
questions.answer: Clean black‑key glissandi, Polish rubato varieties, and seamless voice‑leading in rootless voicings.
questions.rationale: The three works demand virtuosic black‑key technique, nuanced Polish rubato, and advanced harmonic voicing, encapsulating the Diploma’s technical and artistic breadth.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a typical early warning sign of a playing‑related overuse injury for a pianist at the Licentiate level?
choices: Persistent tingling in the fingertips that does not resolve with rest.
Occasional mild fatigue after a thirty‑minute practice session.
Temporary soreness in the forearm that disappears after a warm‑up.
Slight stiffness in the wrists that improves with gentle stretching.
questions.answer: Persistent tingling in the fingertips that does not resolve with rest.
questions.rationale: Persistent tingling indicates nerve irritation that signals an overuse injury rather than normal fatigue.

questions.topic: Bach Partita No. 1 in B-flat, BWV 825
questions.prompt: Which movement of Bach's Partita No. 1 in B-flat major, BWV 825, is known for its constant hand crossings?
choices: Gigue
Praeludium
Sarabande
Allemande
questions.answer: Gigue
questions.rationale: The Gigue of BWV 825 has the left hand crossing over the right throughout; the Praeludium, Allemande and Sarabande have no such crossings.

questions.prompt: When preparing the opening arpeggiated chords of the Chromatic Fantasia, which technical principle from the Octaves and Repeated Notes unit is most critical to avoid tension?
choices: Keep the wrist locked to transfer weight directly to the keys.
Employ a coordinated forearm rotation that releases each chord before the next.
Use a rapid, shallow finger motion for each repeated note.
Maintain a fixed hand span while stretching the fingers to the outer notes.
questions.answer: Employ a coordinated forearm rotation that releases each chord before the next.
questions.rationale: Forearm rotation allows each chord to be released cleanly, preventing accumulated tension.

questions.prompt: A double trill in thirds requires the pianist to execute which of the following coordination?
choices: Alternating trills between hands a minor third apart.
A single trill in the right hand while the left hand sustains a third.
Two independent trills a third apart, each in a different hand.
Simultaneous trills a major third apart in the same hand using alternating fingers.
questions.answer: Simultaneous trills a major third apart in the same hand using alternating fingers.
questions.rationale: The definition of a double trill in thirds is two simultaneous trills a third apart in one hand.

questions.topic: Chopin Ballade No.3 octave practice strategy
questions.prompt: In the climax of Chopin’s Ballade No. 3, the pianist must negotiate rapid octave passages; the recommended practice strategy from the ‘Building Practice Load’ unit is to:
choices: Practice the octaves at full tempo from the start to build endurance.
Substitute the octaves with single‑note lines until the surrounding material is secure.
Isolate the octaves, practice them slowly with exaggerated wrist release, then gradually increase tempo.
Use the pedal continuously to mask any unevenness in the octaves.
questions.answer: Isolate the octaves, practice them slowly with exaggerated wrist release, then gradually increase tempo.
questions.rationale: Slow, isolated work with exaggerated release builds control before tempo is added.

questions.topic: Accompanist balance and chromatic chord listening
questions.prompt: When accompanying a German Lied, the pianist must adjust balance to ensure the vocalist’s diction is clear; the ‘Hearing Chromatic Chords’ unit advises which listening focus?
choices: Prioritize the harmonic root movement in the left hand.
Track the inner voice leading of the chromatic chords while monitoring the singer’s vowel clarity.
Concentrate solely on the dynamic level of the right‑hand melody.
Align the pedal changes strictly with the harmonic rhythm.
questions.answer: Track the inner voice leading of the chromatic chords while monitoring the singer’s vowel clarity.
questions.rationale: Balancing inner voice leading with vocal clarity is the core of the accompanist’s listening task.

questions.prompt: A Licentiate‑level pianist preparing a full recital that includes Baroque, Classical, Romantic, and Lied repertoire must demonstrate which combined competency?
choices: Integrated injury‑preventive technique, stylistic authenticity across eras, and real‑time ensemble balance
Mastery of critical‑edition scholarship for each programmed work
Complete memorisation of the entire recital repertoire without scores
Ability to compose original cadenzas for every concerto on the program
questions.answer: Integrated injury‑preventive technique, stylistic authenticity across eras, and real‑time ensemble balance
questions.rationale: Capstone synthesis of injury prevention, historical style, and ensemble skills covered across all units.

questions.prompt: Which early clinical sign most reliably distinguishes focal dystonia from ordinary fatigue in a professional pianist?
choices: Involuntary curling of the fourth and fifth fingers during rapid passages
Temporary loss of strength after a long rehearsal
Mild soreness in the forearm after practicing octaves
Occasional missed notes when sight‑reading a new work
questions.answer: Involuntary curling of the fourth and fifth fingers during rapid passages
questions.rationale: Focal dystonia typically presents as task‑specific involuntary finger curling, unlike general fatigue.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the International Society for Music Education (ISME) for a pianist at the Fellowship level?
choices: To certify pianists for international competition eligibility
To provide a global network for research, advocacy, and lifelong professional development
To publish a yearly ranking of concert artists
To regulate piano manufacturing standards worldwide
questions.answer: To provide a global network for research, advocacy, and lifelong professional development
questions.rationale: ISME’s mission is to foster worldwide research, advocacy, and continuous development for music educators and performers.

questions.prompt: When preparing a historically informed performance of a C. P. E. Bach keyboard sonata, which source most directly informs the execution of inégales?
choices: The composer’s own preface to the sonata
Czerny’s “School of Velocity” finger exercises
Türk’s “Klavierschule” with its description of unequal notes
Modern Urtext editorial notes on dynamics
questions.answer: Türk’s “Klavierschule” with its description of unequal notes
questions.rationale: Türk explicitly describes the practice of inégales, making his treatise the primary historical guide.

questions.topic: Unifying feature of Chopin Mazurkas Op.59
questions.prompt: What structural feature unifies the three Mazurkas of Op. 59 into a coherent set?
choices: A recurring rhythmic motif derived from the Polish mazurka dance
Identical key signatures across all three
Uniform use of a single tempo marking throughout
A shared tonal plan that moves from B‑major to A‑flat major to F‑sharp minor
questions.answer: A recurring rhythmic motif derived from the Polish mazurka dance
questions.rationale: The three mazurkas share the characteristic mazurka rhythm (strong second‑beat accent and dotted patterns), which binds the set despite differing keys and tempos.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the motion of the Urlinie (fundamental line) in Schenkerian analysis?
choices: It moves by leap.
It moves stepwise descending to the tonic.
It ascends stepwise.
It remains static on the dominant.
questions.answer: It moves stepwise descending to the tonic.
questions.rationale: By definition, the Urlinie is a stepwise descending line that reaches the tonic (scale degree 1̂).

questions.prompt: In Neo‑Riemannian theory, the P operation applied to a C‑major triad yields which chord?
choices: A minor
C minor
E minor
G major
questions.answer: C minor
questions.rationale: The P (parallel) operation changes a major triad to its parallel minor with the same root.

questions.topic: Comprehensive recital preparation at Fellowship level
questions.prompt: A Fellowship‑level pianist planning a recital that includes Schumann’s Piano Quintet in E‑flat, Ravel’s Ondine, Szymanowski’s Étude Op. 4 No. 3, and a reharmonised jazz standard using tritone substitutions must demonstrate mastery of which integrated skill set?
choices: Memorisation of all four works, flawless octave technique, and historical tempo research
Ability to compose an original cadenza for each piece and conduct the ensemble
Collaborative ensemble balance, advanced pedalling, extended technique, and real‑time harmonic re‑imagining
Proficiency in early‑music ornamentation, Baroque continuo realization, and period bowing
questions.answer: Collaborative ensemble balance, advanced pedalling, extended technique, and real‑time harmonic re‑imagining
questions.rationale: The recital demands ensemble coordination, refined pedalling, virtuosic extended techniques, and on‑the‑spot harmonic creativity.

questions.prompt: When preparing three concurrent recital programmes, one of which is thematic, what is the primary factor that determines the rotation schedule for three hours of memorised music?
choices: The total number of pieces across all programmes
The relative technical demands of each programme
The chronological order of composition dates
The length of each individual movement
questions.answer: The relative technical demands of each programme
questions.rationale: Balancing technical load across the three-hour block requires ordering programmes by difficulty to avoid fatigue.

questions.prompt: In the Goldberg Variations, the ground bass repeats every 32 bars and underlies all 30 variations plus the aria. Which structural feature distinguishes the canons from the other variations?
choices: They are the only variations in a minor key
They appear at every third variation and use strict imitation
They employ hand crossings exclusively
They omit the ground bass entirely
questions.answer: They appear at every third variation and use strict imitation
questions.rationale: Every third variation (3, 6, 9 … 27) is a canon at increasing intervals, a defining formal trait.

questions.prompt: When reducing a Figaro ensemble by ear for répétiteur work, which harmonic function should the pianist preserve to maintain the opera's tonal clarity?
choices: The full orchestral texture
The bass line and primary harmonic progressions
All inner voice counter‑melodies
The original dynamic markings of each instrument
questions.answer: The bass line and primary harmonic progressions
questions.rationale: A reduction must keep the functional harmony and bass to support singers and convey the tonal framework.

questions.prompt: In Bach's Goldberg Variations every third variation (3, 6, 9 ... 27) is a canon. How does the interval of these canons change?
choices: It alternates between the fifth and the fourth from one canon to the next
It narrows by one step each time, from the ninth in Variation 3 to the unison
It stays at the octave in every canon, from Variation 3 to Variation 27
It widens by one step each time, from the unison in Variation 3 to the ninth in Variation 27
questions.answer: It widens by one step each time, from the unison in Variation 3 to the ninth in Variation 27
questions.rationale: Variation 3 is a canon at the unison, 6 at the second, 9 at the third ... 27 at the ninth; Variation 30 is the Quodlibet.

questions.prompt: Adapting touch to an unfamiliar piano in thirty minutes requires the pianist to assess which three physical parameters first?
choices: Key dip, hammer velocity, and pedal depth
Key weight, action regulation, and string resonance
Key height, damper timing, and bench distance
Hammer‑to‑string distance, key‑bottom felt, and soundboard stiffness
questions.answer: Key weight, action regulation, and string resonance
questions.rationale: These three parameters most directly affect tone production and must be evaluated before adjusting touch.

questions.prompt: When performing Schubert's D. 960 first movement, the pianist must sustain the long‑range harmonic tension of the opening theme. Which analytical insight guides the shaping of the movement's large‑scale arc?
choices: The movement follows a strict sonata‑allegro with a monothematic exposition
The tonic‑dominant polarity is delayed until the recapitulation
The opening theme's harmonic ambiguity creates a 'floating' tonic that resolves only in the coda
The development section repeats the exposition verbatim
questions.answer: The opening theme's harmonic ambiguity creates a 'floating' tonic that resolves only in the coda
questions.rationale: Schubert's tonic ambiguity postpones resolution, so the performer must pace tension across the entire movement.

questions.prompt: A Professional‑level pianist preparing a full season must coordinate three‑hour recital rotation, Goldberg hand‑crossings, Diabelli double‑fugue architecture, Schubert D.960 long‑range tension, and improvised Mozart concerto cadenzas. Which single practice strategy most efficiently unifies these demands?
choices: Segmented daily blocks assigned to each repertoire category
A unified weekly cycle interleaving technical drills, structural analysis, and performance simulations
Exclusive concentration on the nearest upcoming concert programme
Randomised practice order to prevent predictability
questions.answer: A unified weekly cycle interleaving technical drills, structural analysis, and performance simulations
questions.rationale: Reflects the grade’s emphasis on integrated, interleaved practice across diverse repertoire.

questions.prompt: A pianist preparing for the major international competitions over a three‑year cycle must schedule peak repertoire readiness. Which factor is most critical when aligning the calendar?
choices: Securing the most prestigious venues for each round
Coordinating repertoire peaks with each competition’s required program deadlines
Choosing a single teacher to oversee all preparation phases
Limiting practice to four hours per day to avoid fatigue
questions.answer: Coordinating repertoire peaks with each competition’s required program deadlines
questions.rationale: The three‑year calendar is built around matching peak preparation to each competition’s repertoire deadlines.

questions.prompt: When building hours of non‑repeating competition repertoire, the pianist must ensure each program offers a distinct musical profile. What is the primary strategy to achieve this?
choices: Rotating a fixed set of ten core works across all rounds
Selecting pieces that contrast in style, period, and technical demand for each round
Repeating the same concerto but changing the cadenza each time
Focusing exclusively on contemporary commissions to guarantee novelty
questions.answer: Selecting pieces that contrast in style, period, and technical demand for each round
questions.rationale: Distinct musical profiles are created by varying style, period, and technical demands across programs.

questions.topic: Liszt Transcendental Études touch and voicing
questions.prompt: In the Liszt Transcendental Études, the transition from “Feux follets” to “Wilde Jagd” requires a specific shift in touch and voicing. Which technical adjustment best supports this shift?
choices: Lighten the wrist and increase finger independence for rapid repeated notes
Deepen the key‑bed contact and employ forearm rotation for powerful chords
Adopt a flat finger position to maximize speed in scalar passages
Reduce pedal usage to clarify harmonic changes in both études
questions.answer: Deepen the key‑bed contact and employ forearm rotation for powerful chords
questions.rationale: “Wilde Jagd” demands strong, resonant chords that are produced by deeper key contact and forearm rotation.

questions.prompt: Research on predictors of sight‑reading skill identifies three core components. Which combination correctly lists them?
choices: Aural memory, interval recognition, and rhythmic precision
Pattern recognition, eye‑hand span, and chunking ability
Absolute pitch, harmonic analysis speed, and tempo stability
Finger strength, keyboard geography, and dynamic control
questions.answer: Pattern recognition, eye‑hand span, and chunking ability
questions.rationale: Studies consistently show pattern recognition, eye‑hand span, and chunking as the primary predictors.

questions.prompt: When planning a complete performance of Ligeti’s Études as a recital cycle, the pianist must manage extreme rhythmic complexity across the set. Which rehearsal approach most effectively builds reliability under pressure?
choices: Practicing each étude in isolation at performance tempo from the start
Segmenting the cycle into tempo‑canon groups and rehearsing transitions with a metronome
Recording full run‑throughs daily and reviewing only the final take
Focusing solely on the most technically demanding études and skipping the simpler ones
questions.answer: Segmenting the cycle into tempo‑canon groups and rehearsing transitions with a metronome
questions.rationale: Grouping by tempo canon and drilling transitions with a metronome builds the rhythmic precision needed for the whole cycle.

questions.prompt: During the final rehearsal of a concerto with orchestra, the pianist must coordinate cueing for the cadenza and the orchestral re‑entry. What is the standard protocol for the pianist’s cue to the conductor at the cadenza’s end?
choices: A subtle nod of the head while sustaining the final chord
A clear, upward lift of the right hand from the keyboard
A verbal “ready” spoken toward the conductor
A predetermined click track played through the monitor system
questions.answer: A clear, upward lift of the right hand from the keyboard
questions.rationale: The universally taught cue is an unambiguous upward lift of the right hand signaling the orchestra to re‑enter.

questions.topic: Season‑long planning document for concert artists
questions.prompt: A concert artist preparing a full touring season must coordinate competition deadlines, concerto rehearsals, recital dates, recording sessions, and recovery periods. Which single document best captures all these interlocking demands?
choices: A weekly practice log that records hours spent on each repertoire category.
A repertoire list ranked by personal preference and projected audience appeal.
A master calendar that links competition deadlines, concerto rehearsals, recital dates, recording sessions, and recovery blocks.
A budget spreadsheet projecting income from fees, recordings, and grants.
questions.answer: A master calendar that links competition deadlines, concerto rehearsals, recital dates, recording sessions, and recovery blocks.
questions.rationale: Only a master calendar integrates time‑based commitments across all domains; the other options track only one aspect.

questions.prompt: When preparing a complete Beethoven sonata cycle, which opus numbers constitute the Opus 2 trilogy?
choices: Op. 2 No. 1, No. 2, No. 3
Op. 10 No. 1, No. 2, No. 3
questions.answer: Op. 2 No. 1, No. 2, No. 3
questions.rationale: The Opus 2 set comprises three sonatas (Nos. 1‑3) and is taught as the foundational trilogy for a Beethoven cycle.

questions.prompt: Which pianist's early 20th‑century recordings of the Beethoven sonatas are most cited as a reference for modern complete cycles?
choices: Artur Schnabel
Wilhelm Kempff
Alfred Brendel
Maurizio Pollini
questions.answer: Artur Schnabel
questions.rationale: Schnabel made the first integral recording of the 32 sonatas, establishing a benchmark for later cycles.

questions.prompt: Debussy's twelve Etudes (1915), part of any complete Debussy cycle, are dedicated to the memory of which composer?
choices: Liszt
Rameau
Couperin
Chopin
questions.answer: Chopin
questions.rationale: Debussy dedicated the Douze Etudes 'à la mémoire de Frédéric Chopin'; he had been editing Chopin's works for Durand.

questions.prompt: When programming the complete Well‑Tempered Clavier in two concerts, a common division places the first half of each book in the first concert. How many preludes and fugues are performed in that first concert?
questions.rationale: Each book contains 24 preludes and fugues; half of each book yields 12 + 12 = 24 pieces for the opening concert.

questions.topic: Urtext priority for Brahms late piano pieces
questions.prompt: When a discrepancy arises between the autograph manuscript and the first edition of Brahms’s late piano pieces, which source does Urtext methodology rank highest?
choices: The composer’s corrected proof (Handexemplar)
The autograph manuscript
The first edition as published
A later scholarly edition
questions.answer: The composer’s corrected proof (Handexemplar)
questions.rationale: The Master‑grade unit on editorial decisions teaches that Brahms revised extensively at proof stage, so the composer‑supervised corrected proof (or a first edition reflecting those corrections) supersedes the autograph. The other sources are lower in the editorial hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A pianist maintaining a twenty‑year duo partnership typically coordinates repertoire by which principle?
choices: Alternating solo and duo programs each season
Building a shared core of works while each adds personal projects
Splitting repertoire by composer nationality
Rotating concerti annually
questions.answer: Building a shared core of works while each adds personal projects
questions.rationale: Sustained duos develop a common repertoire foundation and supplement it with individual artistic interests.

questions.topic: Planning a complete Beethoven sonata cycle
questions.prompt: A complete Beethoven sonata cycle often closes with his last three piano sonatas. What are their opus numbers?
questions.rationale: Beethoven's last three sonatas are Op. 109 in E, Op. 110 in A-flat and Op. 111 in C minor; Op. 106 is the Hammerklavier and Op. 126 a set of Bagatelles.

questions.prompt: A tone made only of the partials 600 Hz, 800 Hz and 1000 Hz is usually heard with which pitch?
choices: 200 Hz, the missing fundamental
1000 Hz, the highest partial
800 Hz, the middle partial
600 Hz, the lowest partial present
questions.answer: 200 Hz, the missing fundamental
questions.rationale: 600, 800 and 1000 Hz are harmonics 3, 4 and 5 of 200 Hz, so listeners hear a pitch of 200 Hz although no energy is present there.

questions.prompt: In predictive‑processing accounts of music perception, the brain continuously generates predictions about upcoming events. What term describes the mismatch signal generated when an actual event violates the prediction?
choices: Prediction error
Surprise index
Expectation violation
Prediction residual
questions.answer: Prediction error
questions.rationale: Predictive‑processing frameworks label the discrepancy between prediction and input as a prediction error signal.

questions.prompt: According to Pressing's model of improvisation expertise, which level is defined by the capacity to create novel musical material in real time while preserving structural coherence?
choices: Novice improviser
Competent improviser
Master improviser
Expert improviser
questions.answer: Expert improviser
questions.rationale: Pressing designates the ‘Expert’ level as the stage where improvisers generate new material on the fly without losing formal coherence.

questions.topic: Phase vs period correction in ensemble timing
questions.prompt: In a duo piano performance, the musicians correct timing discrepancies. Which type of correction changes the interval between successive beats rather than the absolute timing of a single beat?
choices: Phase correction
Tempo adaptation
Microtiming alignment
Period correction
questions.answer: Period correction
questions.rationale: Period correction adjusts the period — the interval between successive beats — while phase correction shifts the timing of an individual beat.

questions.prompt: Expert pianists organize memorized repertoire into retrieval structures that facilitate rapid access. Which structural feature allows a pianist to jump directly to a specific section without serial search?
choices: Hierarchical chunking with cue nodes
Linear associative chaining
Distributed semantic network
Episodic timestamp indexing
questions.answer: Hierarchical chunking with cue nodes
questions.rationale: Hierarchical chunking creates cue‑based entry points that enable random‑access retrieval of any section.

questions.prompt: Altering the strike point of a piano hammer changes the spectral content of the tone. Moving the strike point farther from the string’s termination primarily suppresses which partials?
choices: Low‑order partials
High‑order partials
Even‑numbered partials
Odd‑numbered partials
questions.answer: High‑order partials
questions.rationale: Striking nearer a node of higher modes damps those modes, reducing the amplitude of high‑order partials.

questions.topic: Regular temperament theory and physical modelling synthesis
questions.prompt: A researcher wants to compare the perceptual consonance of a 31‑EDO major third (≈387 ¢) with a just‑intoned 5/4 ratio (≈386.3 ¢) using a physical‑modelling piano synthesis that includes hammer‑contact non‑linearity and soundboard radiation. Which combination of theoretical tools is essential to predict the listener’s preference?
choices: Regular temperament mapping, critical‑band roughness curves, and hammer‑contact time model
Equal‑temperament cent conversion, spectral centroid analysis, and duplex‑scaling data
Just‑intonation lattice, MIDI tuning standard, and visual‑learning interface latency
Bohlen‑Pierce scale generator, aliasing filter design, and AI feedback audit log
questions.answer: Regular temperament mapping, critical‑band roughness curves, and hammer‑contact time model
questions.rationale: Predicting preference requires mapping the tuning, modelling auditory roughness via critical bands, and simulating the instrument’s nonlinear hammer‑contact dynamics.

questions.prompt: When evaluating a claim that piano training improves general IQ, which methodological flaw most directly threatens the inference of far transfer?
choices: Lack of an active control group that receives a comparable non‑musical training.
Insufficient sample size to detect medium effect sizes.
Reliance on self‑report questionnaires for outcome measures.
Absence of blinding for participants and assessors.
questions.answer: Lack of an active control group that receives a comparable non‑musical training.
questions.rationale: Without an active control group, any observed IQ gains cannot be attributed specifically to piano training rather than to generic enrichment.

questions.prompt: In a piano competition, judges hear performances in a fixed order. Which bias is most likely to inflate scores for later performers?
choices: Primacy effect, where early performances set an anchor for later ratings.
Recency effect, where the most recent performances are judged more favorably.
Halo effect, where a single outstanding attribute biases overall scores.
Confirmation bias, where judges seek evidence supporting initial impressions.
questions.answer: Recency effect, where the most recent performances are judged more favorably.
questions.rationale: Recency bias causes later performances to be remembered more vividly, leading to higher scores.

questions.prompt: IDyOM models predict listeners' expectancy by combining which two information‑theoretic quantities?
choices: Entropy and surprisal calculated from the score alone.
Pitch‑class distribution and average interval size of the melody.
Long‑term and short‑term predictive distributions learned from a corpus.
Melodic contour complexity and rhythmic density metrics.
questions.answer: Long‑term and short‑term predictive distributions learned from a corpus.
questions.rationale: IDyOM integrates a long‑term model trained on a corpus with a short‑term model that adapts to the current context.

questions.prompt: Continuous key‑position sensors can capture which aspect of touch that discrete MIDI velocity cannot?
choices: Exact key‑down timing measured in microseconds.
Pre‑key‑press finger trajectory captured continuously.
Pedal depth and half‑pedalling position over time.
String vibration amplitude recorded by a bridge sensor.
questions.answer: Pre‑key‑press finger trajectory captured continuously.
questions.rationale: MIDI velocity records only the final speed at key‑bottom, whereas continuous sensors record the entire finger motion before contact.

questions.prompt: Somatosensory inhibition in expert pianists is evidenced by reduced cortical responses to which stimulus during passive tactile stimulation?
choices: Single‑pulse TMS over primary motor cortex during rest.
Median nerve electrical stimulation at the wrist.
Vibrotactile stimulation of the fingertip while the hand is passive.
Auditory click trains presented binaurally.
questions.answer: Vibrotactile stimulation of the fingertip while the hand is passive.
questions.rationale: Studies show attenuated somatosensory evoked potentials to fingertip vibration in expert pianists, indicating inhibitory gating.

questions.topic: Musician's focal dystonia: who is affected
questions.prompt: Musician's focal dystonia is reported to be markedly more common in which group?
choices: Men, by roughly four to one
Children under twelve
Women, by roughly four to one
Amateur players more than professionals
questions.answer: Men, by roughly four to one
questions.rationale: Clinical series (e.g. Altenmüller and Jabusch) report a male predominance of about 4:1, mostly among professional classical musicians; why men are more affected is one of the open questions.

questions.prompt: The Frontier Research capstone requires which combined set of methods to test whether real‑time visual feedback of key‑position trajectories accelerates learning of a complex polyrhythmic passage?
choices: MIDI velocity data only, a simple pre‑post design, basic regression, and subjective listener ratings
Continuous key‑position sensing, a motor‑learning experiment with delayed auditory feedback, IDyOM expectancy modeling, and the expressive‑generation benchmark from Unit 5
Forearm motion capture, a crossover design without control, hidden Markov phrasing model, and the MAESTRO dataset
Force‑sensor keyboards, a single‑session protocol, rule‑based KTH expression system, and the GiantMIDI‑Piano transcription metric
questions.answer: Continuous key‑position sensing, a motor‑learning experiment with delayed auditory feedback, IDyOM expectancy modeling, and the expressive‑generation benchmark from Unit 5
questions.rationale: The capstone specification lists exactly those four methodological components as the required experimental suite.
